caption: Fig. 1. Progression of diagnostic markers in primary and secondary DENV infections in relation to days from symptom onset
description:
Fig. 1 depicts the progression of diagnostic markers (Viral RNA, NS1 Antigen, IgM, and IgG) in relation to days from symptom onset (-4 to 10 days) in primary and secondary DENV infections.

- Primary DENV Infection (Top Panel):
  - Mosquito bite occurs at day -4.
  - Viral RNA rises before symptom onset (around day -2), peaking around day 2 and clearing around day 7-8.
  - NS1 Antigen rises at symptom onset (day 0), peaks around day 4, and decreases towards day 9.
  - IgM appears around day 3 and continues to rise past day 10.
  - IgG appears around day 4 and continues to rise past day 10.
  - A shaded area highlights the 'Risk of shock and haemorrhage' between days ~3 and ~7.

- Secondary DENV Infection (Bottom Panel):
  - Mosquito bite occurs at day -4.
  - Viral RNA rises around day -2, peaks lower and earlier (around day 1), and clears around day 5.
  - Baseline IgG is present and rises rapidly starting around day -2, peaking high and staying elevated.
  - NS1 Antigen shows a lower peak around day 3-4 compared to primary infection.
  - IgM shows a significantly lower and slower response, peaking modestly around day 8.
  - The 'Risk of shock and haemorrhage' window remains highlighted between days ~3 and ~7.

nodes.label: Risk of shock and haemorrhage (Days ~3 to ~7)

section_path: Proposed algorithm for dengue diagnosis in suspected cases
caption: Fig. 2. Proposed algorithm for dengue diagnostics in suspected dengue cases
description: A diagnostic flowchart for suspected dengue cases based on duration of symptoms. Cases ≤ 7 days post symptom onset can undergo RNA NAAT, NS1 ELISA/RDT, or NS1&IgM ELISA/RDT. Cases > 7 days post symptom onset undergo NS1&IgM ELISA/RDT or IgM ELISA/RDT. Diagnostic outcomes are classified as 'Dengue confirmed', 'Probable recent dengue', or 'Dengue not confirmed', with specified follow-up testing (NAAT or seroconversion using convalescent serum collected within 10–14 days) or proceeding to differential diagnosis.

caption: Fig. 3 Proposed dengue diagnostic test menu in a tiered laboratory network (Adapted from (2))
description:
A four-tier pyramid diagram illustrating the proposed dengue diagnostic test menu across a tiered laboratory network:
1. Central or national reference laboratory (Top tier): Test menu includes NAAT, ELISA, virus culture, NGS, PRNT.
2. Regional or provincial laboratory (Second tier): Test menu includes NAAT, ELISA, RDT.
3. District hospital laboratory (Third tier): Test menu includes NAAT, ELISA, RDT.
4. Primary health care centres (Bottom tier): Test menu includes RDT.

caption: Figure 2: Seasonal trend of Dengue Cases in India 2018-2022
description: Line chart displaying the 'Seasonal trend of Dengue Cases in India 2018-2022'. The vertical axis (y-axis) indicates 'No. of Cases' ranging from -5000 to 75000 in increments of 10000. The horizontal axis (x-axis) lists the months from Jan to Dec. The chart compares five years: 2018 (orange line with triangles), 2019 (blue line with x-markers), 2020 (maroon/brown line with asterisks), 2021 (green line with circles), and 2022 (purple line with plus markers). For most years, case counts remain low from January to June (<5000), begin rising in July/August, peak sharply in October or November, and decline by December. The highest peak occurred in October 2022 (~68,000 cases), followed by October 2021 (~63,000 cases), November 2019 (~59,000 cases), October 2018 (~30,000 cases), and October 2020 (~10,000 cases).

caption: Figure 7: Clinical features and lab parameters of Dengue fever
description:
Flowchart representing the clinical features and laboratory parameters of Dengue virus infection, categorized under Clinical manifestations into Symptoms, Sign, and Laboratory.

1. Dengue virus infection -> Clinical manifestations -> Symptoms, Sign, Laboratory.
2. Symptoms:
   - Clinical symptoms & Warming symptoms:
     - Clinical symptoms: Fever, Rash, Headache, Retro-orbital or ocular pain, Myalgia and/or bone pain, Arthralgia.
     - Warming symptoms: Recurrent vomiting, Abdominal pain, Lethargy, Dyspnea, Altered sensorium.
   - Hemorrhagic symptoms: Petechiae, Purpura, Ecchymosis, Epistaxis, Hypermenorrhea, Hematemesis or melena.
3. Sign:
   - Clinical findings: Hepatomegaly, Abdominal tenderness, Pleural effusion, Ascites, Positive tourniquet test.
   - Plasma leakage: Pleural effusion, Ascites, Hypoproteinemia, Hypovolemia, Shock (MAP <65mm Hg).
4. Laboratory:
   - Lab parameters:
     - Haemoconcentration: Haematocrit increase of ≥ 20% from baseline.
     - Thrombocytopenia: Platelet count <1 lac cells per mm³.
     - Leucopenia: Leucocyte count <4000 cells per mm³.
     - Coagulopathy: Raised INR or aPTT (>1.5xULN).
     - Transaminitis.
   - Radiological Investigation:
     - Chest X-ray/Lung Scan: Pleural effusion, Pulmonary edema.
     - Ultrasound abdomen: Acalculous cholecystitis, Ascites.

caption: Figure 11: Algorithms for hospital management for moderate dengue patients with warning signs:
description: Algorithm for hospital management of dengue with warning signs (systolic pressure maintained with signs of reduced perfusion, high Hct ≥ 20% rise from baseline). Initial management starts with isotonic crystalloid solution (7-10 mL/kg for 1 hour). If improvement occurs (monitored by BP, pulse pressure, Hct, urine output, capillary refilling time, pulse rate), IV crystalloid is gradually reduced (5-7 mL/kg/h for 1-2 hours, 3-5 mL/kg/h for 2-4 hours, 2-3 mL/kg/h for 2-4 hours) and stopped at 24-48 hours as clinical improvement is noted. If no improvement, patients with Hct > 45% (suspect persistent capillary leakage) receive IV crystalloid/colloid solution (10 mL/kg for 1 hour), while those with Hct < 45% (suspect severe overt bleed, check Hb) receive blood transfusion (10 mL/kg whole blood / 5 mL/kg packed RBC). If improvement follows these second-line interventions, IV crystalloids are reduced to 7-10 mL/kg/h for 1-2 hours before feeding into the gradual reduction regimen. If no improvement occurs, refractory hypotension is managed with inotropes and managed as severe dengue with decompensated shock (Group C).
